summary: Our project, Green Horizon, is a concept for an app that helps people explore environmental change across Kazakhstan. It brings together indicators such as temperature, precipitation, air quality, and vegetation, displaying them through maps and charts so users can compare places and time periods. By making NASA Earth and climate data easier to explore, Green Horizon can help users spot patterns and investigate how changing conditions may affect ecosystems. The app also aims to show possible future trends, while making clear that forecasts are estimates and that satellite indicators have limitations. This project matters because accessible environmental information can help students, communities, and researchers better understand changes affecting Kazakhstan’s landscapes and ecosystems—and identify where closer monitoring may be useful.
details:
Green Horizon: tracking air and water pollution trends in Kazakhstan with NASA data

What it does and how it works
Green Horizon is a web app that checks whether air and water conditions in Kazakhstan are really changing, or just swinging from year to year. A user picks a place on a map: the whole country, one of 4 macro-regions, one of the 20 regions, a megacity, or a hotspot like the Aral Sea or Lake Balkhash. They can also pick the whole world as a reference. Then they choose an indicator: NO₂, aerosols, dust, SO₂, temperature, precipitation, soil moisture or evaporation.

The app loads monthly NASA time series from Giovanni and Hydrology Time Series and removes the seasonal cycle. It then runs two independent trend tests. The first is OLS regression with a 95% confidence interval, corrected for autocorrelation. The second is Mann–Kendall with Sen’s slope. A trend is called “significant” only if both tests agree. Every result comes with a plain-language explanation, a chart, annual means, and a forecast to 2030 if nothing changes. There are also scenarios showing what happens if the trend is slowed, stopped or reversed.

An AI assistant answers questions in Kazakh, Russian or English. It explains results in simple words, and it gets its numbers from the app’s own statistics functions, so it doesn’t invent them.

Benefits

  • Honest by design. Demo data is off by default. If a region has no real NASA series, the app says “no data” and shows exactly which file to download instead of making up numbers.
  • Every region has a profile from official sources. Area and population come from Kazakhstan’s Bureau of National Statistics (1 March 2025). Air-quality ratings and polluted rivers come from Kazhydromet (H1 2025). Each number links to its source.
  • Accessible. It runs in three languages, works on a phone, and every block has a “?” help button and a guide for first-time users.

Intended impact
We want students, journalists and local officials in Kazakhstan to be able to check claims about pollution and climate themselves, using public satellite data. Some of what we found:

  • Tropospheric NO₂ over Kazakhstan rose significantly in OMI v003 (+0.054×10¹⁵ molec/cm² per decade). In the newer v004 product the rise is weaker and supported by only one test, so we report both.
  • Overall haze tends to rise while dust does not. That points to combustion rather than dust storms.
  • Kazakhstan’s temperature trend (+0.3–0.4 °C per decade, MERRA-2) is larger than the global one (+0.25 °C). That matches Kazhydromet’s +0.33 °C, although 21 years isn’t yet long enough for the Kazakhstan trend to be statistically significant.

These link to known health costs. The World Bank estimates over 10,000 premature deaths a year from air pollution in Kazakhstan, mostly from household heating stoves.

Tools and technologies

  • Front end: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and D3.js (maps and charts), built into a single static file.
  • Statistics: our own JavaScript code for OLS, the t-test, Mann–Kendall, Sen’s slope, and prediction intervals. We verified it against Python’s scipy and pymannkendall.
  • Data pipeline: Python scripts that import Giovanni CSVs (detecting the region and variable from the file header), convert units (K→°C, mm/h→mm/month, kg/m²/s→mm/month) and turn 3-hourly point series into monthly ones. A backup script uses the NASA POWER API, averaging grid points inside region boundaries.
  • Testing: Playwright, in three languages, light and dark themes, and on mobile.
  • Data sources: NASA Giovanni (OMI, MODIS, MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, GLDAS, FLDAS), Hydrology Time Series, NASA POWER, Kazakhstan’s Bureau of National Statistics, Kazhydromet, and peer-reviewed glacier research.
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped write the code and runs the in-app assistant.
  • Hardware: none. It runs in any browser.

Creativity

  • The “detective” approach: the app doesn’t just plot data; it gives a verdict and shows the evidence for it. Two different tests have to agree before the app calls a trend real.
  • Robustness checks built in: two versions of the same NO₂ product side by side, and Kazakhstan compared with the whole planet on one chart.
  • “Where exactly”: for point data, the app shows which parts of a region drive the trend.
  • What-if scenarios for 2030 turn a trend line into a question about policy.

Factors we considered

  • Data honesty: every series shows its dataset, variable ID and unit conversion, and synthetic data is never shown unless the user turns it on.
  • Resolution limits: satellite cells (25–110 km) are bigger than a city. So indicators that can’t separate a city centre from its outskirts are hidden, with an explanation.
  • Statistics: we deseasonalized the data, corrected for autocorrelation, and required at least 9 months of data for a year to count.
  • Language and audience: Kazakh, Russian, and English, for both local users and an international jury.
  • Limits we state openly: the forecast extends a linear trend and doesn’t model new policies. Area averages use rectangles, not exact region borders. Water use by factories can’t be seen from space.
